summary: The builder can start: all required run-time tools and the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server are installed, and the DocumentDB agent skills required to author the sample are present. Several cold answers were confused with Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or other neighbours; those facts are corrected and grounded in the installed skills / Microsoft Learn pages. Missing CLIP-specific docs and a local mongo shell (mongosh) are the main gaps; mongosh is recommended for manual checks but the documentdb MCP server can verify indexes and queries.
summary_points: All operational tooling needed to write, run, and verify the sample is present: python, az, docker, and the documentdb MCP server and the documentdb-* agent skills are installed.

Many cold answers were wrong or outdated because they described Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU throughput / connection host suffix) instead of the new Azure DocumentDB product; the deploy and vector-search skills and Microsoft Learn pages show the correct resource type, CLI usage, connection string shape, billing model, and vector-search APIs.

Vector indexes and queries use DocumentDB's cosmosSearch / $search stage and index kinds (vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann) with createIndex syntax using cosmosSearchOptions; Atlas-style $vectorSearch is not supported.
Local development: there is an official Gateway Docker image exposing Mongo on port 10260 — contrary to the cold answer that said 'no local emulator'.

Gaps: exact driver-level instructions for AAD (OIDC) auth with current PyMongo, and the concrete CLIP-model packaging choice for generating 512-d embeddings are not present in the installed skills/docs and should be decided by the builder.
No missing mandatory MCP servers or skills block the build; some optional CLIs (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) are not installed — mongosh is worth adding for manual database debugging.

tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure subscription/resources if the builder needs to read cluster metadata or to run the Bicep/CLI deploy path (optional).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect Azure control-plane or register provider; but not required to run the sample against the given cluster if DOCUMENTDB_URI is set.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a Cosmos DB (DocumentDB/MongoDB API) account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources under that account).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB; resource type for an Azure DocumentDB cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API version examples in skill: 2025-09-01).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the older Cosmos DB resource model (databaseAccounts) which applies to Cosmos DB service variants; the new Azure DocumentDB product uses a distinct resource type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Examples & quickstarts that use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/az commands would attempt to create the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB account) or fail; deployment templates and CLI commands would be incorrect.
improvements: Add a short note on the Overview or Quickstart page stating: 'For vCore-based Azure DocumentDB clusters use resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).'
Update CLI examples on doc landing pages to show `az resource create --resource-type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters"` or Bicep snippet referencing mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: The management flow for Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters uses standard `az deployment` / Bicep templates or `az resource create` against resource-type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples provided by the documentdb-azure-deployment skill). There is no single core `az cosmosdb` command group that manages mongoClusters; the sample deployment uses Bicep/`az deployment group create` or `az resource create --resource-type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters" --api-version 2025-09-01` (the `cosmosdb` group targets the Cosmos DB databaseAccounts model, not mongoClusters).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The `az cosmosdb` command group manages Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB control-plane); authors conflated Cosmos DB account commands with the new mongoClusters resource.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb docs and examples for Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using `az cosmosdb` commands will not create a mongoClusters resource and will lead to wrong deployment flows or failure when following older quickstarts.
improvements: Add an explicit CLI note in the Azure DocumentDB Quickstart pages: 'To create vCore DocumentDB clusters use `az deployment`/`az resource create` with resource-type `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters`; the `az cosmosdb` group targets databaseAccounts and is not the right command for mongoClusters.'

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { ... kind = "MongoDB" }
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/Terraform should target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep template reference) or the Terraform resource `azurerm_mongo_cluster` / AzAPI targeting the mongoClusters API (documentdb-azure-deployment skill and Terraform references).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' and `azurerm_cosmosdb_account` Terraform resource used for Cosmos DB, not the new mongoClusters resource type and Terraform provider resource for vCore DocumentDB clusters.

confusion_sources.title: Terraform examples that use azurerm_cosmosdb_account for Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Provisioning via the wrong Terraform/Bicep resource would create a different service (Cosmos DB account) or fail; IaC snippets and templates must reference mongoClusters.
improvements: In the Terraform/Bicep quickstart docs, add a clear top-line: 'Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep) or azurerm_mongo_cluster (Terraform) for Azure DocumentDB (vCore); do not reuse azurerm_cosmosdb_account / databaseAccounts snippets.'

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for Cosmos DB: mongodb://<username>@<accountName>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<accountName>@. Username is usually in the form <dbuser>@<accountName> and TLS (ssl=true) is required. Port 10255 (TLS) is used for Cosmos DB MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings are presented as mongodb+srv or mongodb URIs for the mongoClusters resource, e.g. mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (see documentdb-azure-deployment). The host suffix and SRV form differ from older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts endpoints.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the cosmos 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255' pattern used by Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; DocumentDB vCore clusters use different hostnames (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com, often SRV) and a different control-plane model.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection examples showing account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port/URI form will fail client connections and cause confusion when constructing MongoClient URIs; developer instructions must use the cluster's actual connection string (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as provided in the environment.
improvements: Add an explicit example in the quickstart showing the SRV form returned by `mongoClusters` and a sample line telling builders to read the cluster string from DOCUMENTDB_URI.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is provisioned throughput measured in Request Units per second (RU/s) or autoscale RU/s; there is also a serverless option ... additionally, Azure offers vCore-based dedicated cluster (M-series) options for dedicated MongoDB-compatible clusters (vCore billing).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers (M10..M200) / vCore-like provisioning and predictable compute + storage pricing; it is distinct from Cosmos DB's RU-based model (the latter is the RU/serverless model). DocumentDB supports dedicated compute tiers and the M-series list (M10..M200) — pricing & scale are vCore-based (documentdb-azure-deployment and Learn pages).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed Cosmos DB's RU model (request units) with the new vCore-based Azure DocumentDB offering; these are different billing models for different services.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder used RU/s assumptions (throttling, retry strategies, pricing expectations), they would pick wrong instance types and be surprised by billing or capability differences; use the M-series compute-tier guidance instead.
improvements: Add a short decision guide on the product overview page clarifying: 'Use Azure DocumentDB (vCore / M-series) for vCore-based clusters; use Azure Cosmos DB for RU-based or serverless models.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Common auth for the MongoDB API is SCRAM (username/password) using the Cosmos DB account keys ... Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integration for the MongoDB API is limited/preview and not universally available; if Entra auth is supported you must obtain an AAD access token and present it via the driver’s SASL/OAUTHBEARER ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports SCRAM (SCRAM-SHA-256) credentials and also supports Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication with RBAC for applications and managed identities; driver usage for Entra typically uses an OIDC-style authMechanism (examples name `MONGODB-OIDC` or `MONGODB-AAD` and recommend using managed identities). The documentdb-security skill provides guidance and links to official docs showing Entra + RBAC flows (security-entra-rbac.md).

grounding_links.title: Use Microsoft Entra ID and role-based access control

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer understated Entra support (treated it as preview) and speculated on driver mechanisms; the installed security docs explicitly describe Entra + RBAC and recommend OIDC-style driver auth, but drivers may have slightly different mechanism names and builder should check current driver docs.

confusion_sources.title: Old forum threads that treated AAD integration as preview for Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD is unavailable, they may implement long-lived SCRAM passwords or Key Vault flows instead of using managed identities; this is a security risk and undermines best practices.
improvements: Add a cookbook page that shows a concrete PyMongo / Node example using managed identity / AAD token exchange (exact driver config and sample code) and name the authMechanism string to use against the current stable driver.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python, use pymongo). Do NOT use the azure-cosmos SDK for MongoDB API access — the MongoDB wire protocol is served and you should use MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo for Python). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB client SDK; azure-cosmos SDK is not for the MongoDB API. The documentdb-driver skill enforces the singleton MongoClient pattern and driver best practices.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Newer/documentdb clusters support vector index algorithms such as IVF, HNSW and DiskANN ... Typical index creation is done with the MongoDB-style createIndex API on the collection specifying a vector index on the embedding field. Example (pseudo-command): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_ivf', vectorIndexType: 'ivf', vectorIndexConfig: { dimension: 512, nlist: 1024 } }) — exact option names may differ
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds DiskANN, HNSW and IVF (recommendations depend on scale). Indexes are created with createIndex but the field type is `cosmosSearch` and options live under `cosmosSearchOptions` (example: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, { cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-ivf', dimensions:512, similarity:'COS', nlist:1024 } })). Vector query uses $search with cosmosSearch. See documentdb-vector-search and vector-create-diskann-index resources.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic Atlas-style or hypothetical option names (`'vector'` / `vectorIndexType`) instead of DocumentDB's `cosmosSearch` field and `cosmosSearchOptions` syntax.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Atlas vector-search docs showing $vectorSearch syntax

confusions.build_risk: Using Atlas-style index API or wrong option names will fail or create a non-vector index; the index must be created with `cosmosSearchOptions` and matching dimensions.
improvements: On any vector-search quickstart include a minimal `db.collection.createIndex` example with `cosmosSearchOptions` and a note: 'Do not use Atlas $vectorSearch or field name `vector` — use `cosmosSearch` and supply cosmosSearchOptions.'

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) does not expose the same built-in full-text/hybrid search as a dedicated search service; for full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search you typically integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB includes native `cosmosSearch` capabilities that support lexical (text) + vector search and hybrid queries via the `$search` aggregation stage. You do not have to push to Azure Cognitive Search for hybrid text+vector queries. See documentdb-vector-search and vector-knn-query resources.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described older patterns or the Cosmos DB NoSQL API's integration points; it assumed no native vector/text facility, but DocumentDB provides `cosmosSearch` as first-class functionality.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search integration examples for Cosmos DB NoSQL

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes no native hybrid search, they might add unnecessary synchronization to Cognitive Search and increase complexity/cost.
improvements: Add a short note near vector-search docs: 'DocumentDB includes native text+vector (cosmosSearch) functionality — external search services are optional for advanced indexing/ingestion scenarios only.'

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported wire protocol/version depends on the account SKU but modern deployments support up to recent MongoDB server wire versions ... Many administrative and server-side features of a native MongoDB server are not available ... some aggregation operators or latest server-only features are missing or behave slightly differently.
confusions.grounded_answer: Microsoft docs and compatibility pages state Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0 and implements ~99% of MongoDB operators; some administrative commands and a few server-only features are intentionally not exposed by the managed service (see compatibility guide).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn compatibility pages (queried via learn_microsoft_docs_search)

grounding_links.title: MongoDB compatibility and supported wire protocol versions

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer was vague; Learn pages confirm explicit supported versions (5.0–8.0) and the managed-service limitations on admin commands.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a different wire version could cause driver incompatibilities; builders must target drivers compatible with the service's advertised wire protocol (5–8).
improvements: Explicitly list the supported wire protocol versions on the product overview and quickstarts so builders can pin driver versions reliably.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator that reproduces the MongoDB API behavior of Azure Cosmos DB; for local development run a local MongoDB server (docker run -p 27017 ...) The official Azure Cosmos DB Emulator historically does not support the MongoDB API feature set.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is an official DocumentDB Gateway Docker image intended for local development exposing the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260; the documentdb-local-deployment skill documents the Gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and port 10260 with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 for local tests.

grounding_links.title: Local Gateway image and ports (Gateway on 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer referenced Cosmos DB's limitations and the Cosmos DB emulator; DocumentDB (the new product) provides a local Gateway image to reproduce behavior.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB emulator limitations for MongoDB API

confusions.build_risk: If the builder believes no local option exists, they may be forced to run everything against the live cluster during development; using the Gateway image improves dev iteration speed.
improvements: Update local-development docs to highlight the Gateway image, port 10260 and TLS guidance, so builders won't default to ephemeral local Mongo images.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported on MongoDB API accounts that advertise a compatible server version ... verify support on the target account before relying on it.
confusions.grounded_answer: Learn compatibility pages show `$changeStream` aggregation stage is supported in Azure DocumentDB for supported server versions (documented in the compatibility matrix). No special toggle is required beyond using an account that advertises a compatible MongoDB version.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The dedicated MCP server for this service is the 'documentdb' MCP server ... The general Azure MCP server does not automatically provide documentdb-specific data-plane inspection tools; use the documentdb MCP server’s tooling/profile.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the `documentdb` MCP server for data-plane tasks (it is present in inventory). The general `azure` MCP server exists but does not substitute for documentdb data-plane tools.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft’s hosted DocumentDB service was the precursor name; that platform evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. 'DocumentDB' was the original name ... Azure Cosmos DB now supports multiple APIs, including the MongoDB-compatible API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Clarified: The new product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and was later renamed to Azure DocumentDB; it is distinct from the older 2014–2017 'DocumentDB' that became Azure Cosmos DB and is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) are separate services (vCore vs RU models).

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the historical product names; Learn pages clarify that the vCore product was previously called 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and then renamed 'Azure DocumentDB'.
confusions.build_risk: Minor naming confusion only; could lead to referencing wrong docs if the builder searches for the older name.
improvements: Add a short 'names and timelines' paragraph on the product landing page listing: original DocumentDB -> Azure Cosmos DB (2017) -> vCore product rebranded to Azure DocumentDB (year) and how they differ.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Cosmos DB’s proprietary storage and query engine which implements the MongoDB wire protocol for the MongoDB API. ... use MongoDB drivers unchanged for normal CRUD/aggregation operations, but test advanced features and admin operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the project is public) and exposes the MongoDB wire protocol — applications use standard MongoDB drivers. The engine being open-source may allow on-prem or multi-cloud runs, but application-level MongoDB drivers remain the same; only a few administrative operations differ in a managed service.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's proprietary engine rather than the new DocumentDB engine (open-source) powering the vCore product.
confusions.build_risk: Minimal for basic CRUD/aggregation; risk appears only if the builder relies on server admin commands or expects Cosmos DB-specific behaviors.
improvements: Clarify the engine relationship on the overview page: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine; applications use MongoDB drivers unchanged.'

confusions.question: What database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name 'sample_retail_11' for all collections and operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run-environment and prompt_md specify using the database `sample_retail_11` for all sample-created collections.

confusions.question: How should the sample store 512-dimension float embeddings as BSON binary with subtype 0x09 from Python?
confusions.cold_answer: Encode the float32 vector to little-endian bytes and wrap with bson.Binary with subtype 0x09. Example code: bson.Binary(np.array(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes(), subtype=0x09).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: store the float32 bytes as BSON binary with subtype 0x09. This is the recommended approach in the sample guidance and matches the vector storage expectations for DocumentDB vector indexes.

confusions.question: What createIndex call will the sample use to request an IVF vector index for the embedding field?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB-style createIndex on the embedding field with vector index options. Example (pseudo-code): db.products.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_ivf', vectorIndexType: 'ivf', vectorIndexConfig: { dimension: 512, nlist: 1024 } } ). The sample will call collection.create_index(...) with equivalent options via PyMongo.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: the correct DocumentDB pattern is to call createIndex with the field type `cosmosSearch` and pass vector index options under `cosmosSearchOptions`, e.g. db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, { cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-ivf', dimensions: 512, similarity: 'COS', nlist: 1024 } }). See vector-create-diskann-index and vector-search docs.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic 'vector' typed index and option names which match Atlas or hypothetical APIs, rather than the DocumentDB `cosmosSearch` + `cosmosSearchOptions` shape.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tried to call the wrong option names via PyMongo, index creation would fail; use the `cosmosSearchOptions` wrapper and ensure dimensions/similarity match embeddings.
improvements: Add a small, copy-paste createIndex snippet on the vector-search quickstart that shows the `cosmosSearchOptions` shape for IVF/HNSW/DiskANN so builders don't invent Atlas-like option keys.

confusions.question: Which image-embedding model will the sample use to get 512-dimensional vectors?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a CLIP model that produces 512-d vectors, e.g. Hugging Face 'openai/clip-vit-base-patch32' via transformers: from transformers import CLIPProcessor, CLIPModel; processor = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32'); model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32') — produce a normalized 512-d float32 embedding.
confusions.grounded_answer: could_not_verify
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The installed DocumentDB skills and Microsoft docs don't prescribe a CLIP checkpoint; the prompt-review assumed a reasonable CLIP model but no installed skill or Learn doc states the exact model to use.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder picks a CLIP variant that outputs a different dimensionality (e.g. 768 or 1024), the embedding dimension will mismatch the index and silently return wrong results; the builder must pick a model that outputs 512 dims or change the index to match.
improvements: Add a small 'AI model' guidance doc in the sample template that specifies a recommended checkpoint name, its embedding dimension, and the minimal preprocessing steps (resize / normalization) to avoid dimension mismatches.

confusions.question: How will the sample issue the vector search query to get top-8 nearest neighbors after encoding a query image?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will rely on the server-side vector search facility exposed through the MongoDB API. It will present the query vector as BSON binary subtype 0x09 and call the collection's vector search operator (example pseudo-call): collection.find({ '$vectorSearch': { 'field': 'embedding', 'vector': <Binary>, 'k': 8, 'algorithm': 'ivf' } }) or use the corresponding aggregate stage if required. If exact syntax differs, fall back to client-side similarity ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong: DocumentDB uses the `$search` aggregation stage with `cosmosSearch` for vector queries. The correct aggregate looks like: db.products.aggregate([ { $search: { cosmosSearch: { path: 'embedding', vector: <binary-or-array>, k: 8, lSearch: <n>, filter: { ... } } } }, { $project: { ..., score: { $meta: 'searchScore' } } } ]). The Atlas-style `$vectorSearch` operator is not supported. See vector-knn-query.md.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used Atlas or other-vector-store syntax (`$vectorSearch`) instead of DocumentDB's `$search` + `cosmosSearch` stage.
confusions.build_risk: Using $vectorSearch or a wrong operator will produce runtime errors; the builder must construct a `$search` aggregation stage with cosmosSearch options and ensure `lSearch >= k`.
improvements: Include a single copy-paste example of the `$search` aggregation with `cosmosSearch` in the sample README (with k=8 and a recommended lSearch), so builders don't reuse Atlas syntax.

information_gaps.title: Exact PyMongo / driver auth flow for Microsoft Entra (OIDC)
information_gaps.description: Installed skills/documentation explain that Entra ID + RBAC is supported and recommend OIDC-style driver auth (security-entra-rbac.md), but none of the installed skills or Learn snippets documents the exact PyMongo (or other language driver) options / code to obtain an AAD token and pass it to the driver (e.g., which authMechanism string is required, whether PyMongo supports it natively, or specific code samples). I searched: documentdb-security resources, documentdb-connection, and Microsoft Learn compatibility pages and found no exact PyMongo code sample for AAD auth.

information_gaps.title: CLIP checkpoint and preprocessing canonicalization
information_gaps.description: No installed skill prescribes the exact CLIP model checkpoint and precise preprocessing (resize, normalization, pooling) to guarantee 512-d outputs for the sample. I looked in the prompt_review and installed skills; none state a single recommended HF checkpoint and the dependent PyTorch/transformers package pins.

information_gaps.title: Driver API mapping for createIndex cosmosSearchOptions via PyMongo
information_gaps.description: The vector-index examples are visible in the documentdb-vector-search skill as JS-like snippets (db.collection.createIndex). There is no explicit PyMongo code sample showing how to pass the `cosmosSearchOptions` options object via the PyMongo create_index() call; I checked the vector-search skill resources and did not find a PyMongo snippet.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when referring to the vCore Azure DocumentDB cluster in ARM/Bicep/az commands.

Create vector indexes using createIndex with field type 'cosmosSearch' and provide vector options under 'cosmosSearchOptions' (kind: vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann), and query with $search + cosmosSearch; do not use Atlas $vectorSearch or a plain 'vector' field type.

Read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and use it as-is (do not commit or log it); the deployment skill shows the SRV/host suffix and the requirement for TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256.

Store embeddings as float32 little-endian bytes wrapped in bson.Binary with subtype 0x09 (e.g., bson.Binary(np.array(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes(), subtype=0x09)) and ensure the index dimensions match the embedding vector length.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for interactive debugging and ad-hoc checks. Simplest: `npm i -g mongosh` (or install the platform package from MongoDB distribution) so developers can run local and live-cluster checks.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample; only add if you plan to include azd-based app deploy recipes. If desired, follow azd installation docs (install via package manager) or use az directly.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Optional: add bicep if the team wants to author and validate Bicep templates locally; the simplest route is `az bicep install` or follow the Bicep install docs. Not required to build the sample app against an existing cluster.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
